_about.what: Data behind site-management-roadmap.html. Every ticket object has two halves: STATIC fields authored from the ticket scope files, and LIVE fields (pmTicketNumber / pmStatus / pmAssignee / pmUrl) pmTicketNumber is filled in; pmUrl is deliberately left null because this page is public.
_about.naming: RENAMED IN THE v2 SCOPE PASS. The initiative is FIELD MANAGEMENT, and every piece of content here says so. The filenames, the source folder and the published URL deliberately keep their original spelling so no link breaks — the same call the source folder made about its own name. Content renames; paths do not. The SM- and S- key prefixes stay too, and they are no longer an abbreviation of the module's name: SM- means Field-Management-specific, S- means it serves the whole platform. Where "Site Access" appears, that is the existing licensed feature this module absorbs: it becomes an "Access" option on a Site rather than a module of its own, and the site object it already owns is the one the work-context engine reuses.
_about.authority: parent-site-management-mvp.md and the per-ticket files in the same folder are the source of truth for every STATIC field. Do not invent tickets or dependencies here.
_about.axes: TWO INDEPENDENT AXES, and conflating them is the mistake the old tier system made. TIER is timing — A ships with MVP, B builds in parallel, C comes after, D is backlog. PREFIX is ownership — SM- is Field-Management-specific, S- serves the whole platform. A ticket's prefix does not determine its tier: S-01 and S-06 are S-tickets in Tier A, SM-05 is an SM-ticket in Tier C. Prefix is derived from the key in the page; it is not a stored field.
_about.slices: Two tickets are SPLIT across tiers, because their parts land at different times and edges point at specific parts. A split ticket appears once per slice, as its own node, with a lowercase suffix on a shared key stem — S-04a / S-04b / S-04c, S-02a / S-02b. `sliceGroup` is the stem, `sliceGroupTitle` the ticket's own name, and `sliceLabel` what that slice is called in the scope files. The page groups the siblings visually and lists them in each other's panels. The suffix is a slice letter, never a tier letter. SM-06 was a third until the Oct 1 check-in: its two slices collapsed back into one node when the entry gate was dropped, so SM-06 now carries no slice fields.
_about.structure: Graph structure comes from each ticket's dependsOn (hard prerequisites) and relatedTo (relationships that do not gate the target). edgeMeta only decorates those edges with a kind + note; an edge with no edgeMeta entry defaults to kind 'required'. Stage/layer position is computed in the page by longest-path layering, so adding a dependency re-lays-out the graph automatically.
_about.nonTicketFields: Four fields carry things the edge model cannot. `blockedByAlso` is an array of non-ticket blockers (a pending decision, a pre-build confirmation) — real gates with no card to draw an arrow from. `blocksNote` qualifies an empty Blocks list. `related` is a display-only relationship list that deliberately draws NO edge, so a ticket that blocks nothing still reads as connected to the tickets it touches. `mergedFrom` records a ticket that was folded into this one and no longer has a card.
_about.conflicts: Top-level `conflicts` records cross-ticket disagreements that are flagged and NOT fixed. Each names the tickets it sits between; the page derives a warning chip on each of those cards and lists the conflict in full in the About view. Nothing here is a decision. The array is currently EMPTY — the one conflict on record, over who owned the competency gate, was resolved and then the gate itself was dropped: training is read from the training matrix and shown as a badge, and nothing in Field Management blocks on it. The feature stays in place because the next disagreement will want it.
_about.pending: Top-level `pending` records questions that are deliberately UNRESOLVED and waiting on product leadership. They are not conflicts — nobody disagrees, the answer simply has not been given. Each names the tickets it lands on; the page derives a pending chip on those cards and states each item in full in the About view. NOTHING HERE IS A DECISION, and nothing in this file should be edited to pre-empt one.
_about.order: Within a stage, cards render in the order tickets appear in this array. That order is chosen to minimise connector crossings — reorder deliberately. The register groups by tier and preserves the same order inside each group.

_refresh.summary: Claude refreshes this file; the browser never calls BIS PM. A page opened from file:// cannot fetch a sibling JSON, so the HTML carries an inline mirror of this file.
steps: 2. For every ticket where pmTicketNumber is NOT null, call mcp__pmMCP__getTicketDetails with that number.
3. Write the result into that ticket's LIVE fields: pmStatus (the PM status string), pmAssignee (display name or null), pmUrl (the BIS PM ticket URL). Leave every STATIC field untouched.
4. For tickets that have since been created in BIS PM, set pmTicketNumber first (find it with mcp__pmMCP__getTicketList or getTicketsByGroup), then do step 3. pmUrl is what makes a card clickable.
5. Set meta.lastRefreshed to an ISO-8601 timestamp. The page renders it in the masthead; null renders as 'never'.

7. CRITICAL — also rewrite the inline mirror inside site-management-roadmap.html, between the ROADMAP-DATA:BEGIN and ROADMAP-DATA:END comment markers. The two must stay byte-identical, or a double-clicked page will show stale data. The page footer reports which source it actually used.
notes: Every LIVE field is null on purpose, so every card shows the muted "#—" placeholder chip. This page is published to a public repo. Ticket numbers are shown; the ticket URLs are deliberately left null, so no card links into BIS PM from the open web. Do not add pmUrl without being asked.
A split ticket is ONE ticket in BIS PM, not three. When S-04 or S-02 gets a number, the same number goes on every slice node of that ticket.
Every ticket in the initiative now exists in BIS PM and carries its number here. pmUrl stays null on all of them for the public-repo reason above.
Nothing in the HTML fetches anything at runtime except Google Fonts. There is no build step.

meta.title: Field Management — build order and dependencies
meta.standfirst: Twelve child tickets and the MVP parent, on two independent axes. Tier is timing; the SM- / S- prefix is ownership. Two of the twelve are split across tiers and appear once per slice, so the map carries sixteen cards. This is the dependency spine: what has to land first, what builds alongside it, and what explicitly does not gate the MVP.

standaloneLabel.label: Independent — nothing blocks them, they block nothing

A.label: Tier A
A.name: Ships with MVP
A.note: Blocks release. The MVP does not ship until every one of these lands.

B.label: Tier B
B.name: Parallel build
B.note: Does not block the MVP, and is active now.

D.label: Tier D
D.name: Backlog
D.note: Not scheduled. Nothing sits here in v2 — the two tickets that did were closed or moved out of the initiative.

SM.label: SM-
SM.name: Field Management
SM.note: Specific to this module. Field Management drives it and Field Management's team builds it. The letters are legacy — they are not an abbreviation of the module's name.

S.label: S-
S.name: System-wide
S.note: Serves the whole platform. Field Management is the reason it gets prioritised, not its home.

required.label: Hard prerequisite
required.note: The target cannot be built until the source lands.

partial.label: Conditional — part only
partial.note: A real dependency that gates only part of the target. The rest of that ticket is not blocked, so this line must not be read as a whole-ticket gate.

shared.label: Shared component — built once
shared.note: Not a gate in either direction. The two tickets need the same piece, and whichever ships first builds it while the other reuses it. The arrow shows the order the plan currently expects, not a prerequisite.

pending.title: Locations — import names, import with people, or a live link?
pending.what: The MVP has no Location import: a Site is deliberately a place that is not a Location, and copying Locations in would duplicate every one of them once a live link lands. The room then leaned back towards importing Location names, optionally with their people, and possibly a live link instead.
pending.state: This is the known day-one gap. A client whose places are all Locations — one has 52 branches — gets less on day one until live-linked Locations land, and they cannot slip far behind the MVP.

pending.title: External people as a platform-wide record — and how it is charged
pending.what: In the MVP an external person is a record in one portal, with training added by hand. The bigger version is one person carrying their own documents between portals, so a contractor uploads once and every client's portal can read it. That raises where it lives, how the same person is recognised across portals, the security of searching for them — and pricing, which is per user today.
pending.state: The MVP slice is scoped to one portal and does not depend on the answer. The full ticket cannot be written without it.

pending.title: Scoped permissions in the rest of the platform — alongside system roles, not replacing them
pending.what: Field Management's permissions are a clean sheet — they do not read from or change today's system roles. The open question is whether that clean sheet is then offered in other modules alongside the system roles that already exist, rather than as a replacement for them, with folders, forms and assets next.
pending.state: The build is the same either way, which is why it is not blocking. What changes is how much else is designed against it, and how carefully.

pending.title: Offline — sync, or degrade?
pending.what: Either the obligation set syncs to the device, or the mobile surface degrades to something that works with no signal. One client runs 50–80% no-signal sites; at another, operators go days without connectivity. Both answers are real products and they are not the same build.
pending.state: This is the blocking decision on the mobile ticket, and the object-scan ticket is held by it too. It needs its own working session — roughly half an hour — closer to build.

pending.title: The who's-on-site list — in the MVP, or just after?
pending.what: A read-only, auto-refreshing list of who is on site, for emergencies, with a flag for overdue sign-outs. Where it lives is now settled: sign-in and sign-out, the list itself, timers and notifications are Field Management's, moved over from the existing access feature with their history migrated. What is not settled is whether it ships in the MVP or immediately after it.
pending.state: Only the timing is open. The earlier version of this question — keep it or cut it — was answered by folding the access feature in, and it stays the tenth interface item in the parent either way. Only one client of fifteen asked for live presence, for muster, which is the argument for "just after" rather than for cutting it.

pending.title: One-off work — build it in Field Management, or link to Folders?
pending.what: Rituals are set once and left to run, so one-off work is a task added or a form assigned inside a Site or Job. The objection raised is commercial rather than technical: on-demand forms inside Field Management remove the reason a client pays for Folders. Either Field Management builds the one-off path, or it links out to the module that already owns it.
pending.state: Not decided, and it needs a company decision rather than a product one — it sits with the Folders and Assets overlap below. What is needed either way is assigning to a whole Site, to individuals, and from a supervisor to their crew.

pending.title: The overlap with Folders and Assets, now that the module is paid
pending.what: Field Management is a paid module with a free trial period. For some clients it may make Folders redundant — on-demand forms — and Assets too, where Assets is used only to hold sites. Which of those overlapping parts Field Management builds is a company decision, not a design one.
pending.state: Needed before the overlapping parts are built. It is the same decision the one-off-work question above is waiting on, which is why the two are carried separately rather than merged: one is a scope question, the other is a pricing one.

The mobile surfaces render work-context state and hold the Site and Job list, so there is nothing to render until the engine exists.
A submission needs something to be attributed to, and the roll-up structure to count through.
"A named set of Sites and Jobs" has no meaning until the work-context engine exists.

External people are held against a work context, and the Site Access visitors carried over by the merge are what the record has to hold on day one.

Nothing else in the list functions without the work-context engine.

The whole slice is the existing form field learning to pre-fill from a Crew.

Crew breakdowns, view-without-edit and work-context membership all hang off Crew.

Named in the parent's Blocked by line.

The full model extends the "Can view" grant foundation — subject plus scope, grants only add — rather than replacing it.
Read-only access over a chosen set of Sites and Jobs is part of who can open Field Management at launch.

Who may sign off what is a grant with a subject and a scope, which is the full model rather than the read-only slice. Until it exists a simpler stopgap is needed — a setting on the form template, or a crew.

Per-person obligations on any Site or Job. Signing in is what makes that day's rituals owed — Sites as well as Jobs, not just Jobs — and counts-per-person reads presence. A ritual counted per work context, on its own calendar, is not blocked by it.
The supervisor's "mark present" action is this checklist — the one supervisor action the research evidences.
The later attachment points — meetings, form witnesses, tasks — all write to the presence record this slice builds.
A meeting needs the "signed" proof level, which moved into this slice. A supervisor's tick is not proof that someone received a talk.

The same signing component, built once. It is already being designed through another ticket, reusing the existing mobile signature component, so neither of these two builds it from scratch — which is why this line is a shared piece, not a gate in either direction.

The compliance badge beside the missing-forms count, and the per-person badge on the supervisor surface — informational, and it links out to that person's own training page rather than copying it.
The compliance count sits beside the missing-forms count on the index and the work-context view, as a separate number that never merges into it.
A badge beside each name on the crew list — one of the three places people are listed, and the one Crew owns.

tickets.title: Work contexts: Site + Job
tickets.summary: The thing an admin watches — one engine, two kinds. A Site is a place that keeps going and archives; a Job is a piece of work with a start, a stage and a close-out. A Job can sit at a Site, inheriting its address and working days while keeping its own dates and rituals, or span several. Each holds people, what they owe and what came in, and answers one question: current, or N outstanding? Built on the existing Site Access site object rather than a second one, so existing sites and their visitors are there on day one — and that feature stops being a module of its own: an Access option on a Site opens its screens, unchanged.
tickets.mergedFrom: The standalone Job ticket was folded into this one in the v2 pass. Job is now a kind inside the work-context engine rather than an object with its own card, which is why the map has no separate Job node — and why Job moved from a parallel build into the MVP with it.
tickets.mvpNote: MVP-blocking. Nothing else in the initiative functions without it.
tickets.boundary: Assets keep things — vehicles, equipment, properties. A work context keeps place, work and who owes what. Sites never nest, and a Job never owns a Site. Dispatch and scheduling stay out: people pick the Site or Job they are on from a list, and that choice is the visit. Improving the access feature's screens stays out too — they move behind the Access option exactly as they are. A group above Sites and Jobs is not built in the MVP either; the engine only has to leave room for one.
openQuestions: What goes in the close-out evidence pack, and in what format — one PDF per Job, an export, or both?
Can a client change their engagement label after setup — Job to Project, say — once data exists?
Setup: Sites and Jobs in one pass, or one kind at a time? Answered provisionally as one kind at a time; confirm before build.
One person, several Jobs in a day. The admin sees gaps per Job, and the tentative rule is that anyone assigned to Jobs picks at least one per working day. Parked.
Dev, before estimating: what does the Site Access site object carry today, and can it gain working days, a lifecycle and a parent link without changing anything for existing Site Access clients?
Dev: import-from-Assets picker usability at 172 rows, duplicate names, the same Asset imported twice, and whether the copy is one-time or keeps a reference to its source.
Dev: can counting at the most specific context and rolling up be computed on read without a performance problem at 52-branch scale?
Timing risk worth checking before build: reusing the Site Access site object brings back a clash with the two Site Access scan-in/out tickets that the earlier build-a-new-object plan had removed.
scope: The engine — two kinds, one label per kind from a short list written by BIS, and navigation that follows the labels a client picked
One shared base that each kind extends, with room above it for a group level later — neither needs a redesign to add
Site — name, exact address, working days set as a company default and overridden only where a site differs, presence, archive
Job — name, optional address, start date, optional expected end, stage, close-out and the exportable evidence pack
A Job at a Site inherits its address, working days and its Access setting, and keeps its own dates, stage, close-out and rituals; a ritual both carry is owed once

Access — the existing access feature becomes an option on a Site that opens its own screens, with nothing done to them: off by default, on for anyone who has it today, and its compliance requirements untouched
Sign-in on any Site or Job — picking one from the list is the sign-in, and it is what makes that day's rituals owed
Owner, manager and supervisor as information-only fields — nothing is assigned, permitted or routed through them
Counting — a form counts toward the most specific work context and rolls up; a Job spanning Sites counts toward the Job only
Setup — create from scratch, or import from Assets by name only, leaving the original Asset untouched. Sites and Jobs are created on the web in the MVP
No archiving a Site or closing a Job while anything is outstanding — the admin cleans up first
tickets.evidence: There is no single replacement for "site" — there are six, and no majority. Compliance attaches to a job at 4 of 14 companies, to a place at 3, and to a person, an asset, a crew or a document at the rest. Four clients tried Assets as an organisational construct and abandoned it; product leadership's decisive point is that an asset can only have one assigned person, and an asset used as a site cannot say who is on it or what is owed. Job is the largest single anchor in the corpus, and renaming a Site gives you a job that cannot end.

tickets.title: Crew
tickets.summary: Who is answerable for a work context, as distinct from who happened to do the work. A crew exists on its own, is assigned to Sites and Jobs — several Jobs at once — and remembers who was in it on any given day. Assignment is standing; presence is daily. Membership is dated, because a record layer that shows last month's crew as today's crew is quietly falsifying the thing it exists to prove. A crew is never a condition of anything: people can be added to a Site or a Job directly, and nobody needs a crew to sign in. Permissions stay deliberately coarse: none, read-only, full edit.
tickets.mvpNote: MVP-blocking. It is also the stopgap that keeps the supervisor view out of the permissions ticket's way — a supervisor sees the work contexts their crew is assigned to, built entirely from here, and access starts crew-based for the same reason.
tickets.boundary: Not dispatch and not an org chart. Crew says who is answerable, not who does what today — presence decides the day. Owner, manager and supervisor on a work context are information-only fields and belong to the work-context ticket, not here. Crews that include external people, and crew as a universal assignment target across forms, folders and shared tasks, are real and evidenced but come after the MVP.
openQuestions: Can a person be in more than one crew at once? Someone covering two crews in a day is plausible.
Who can edit crew membership, and is that different from today's attendance? A supervisor adjusting who is here today is attendance; permanently changing who is in the crew is this ticket.

Where does Crew live — inside this module, in Users, or on its own? The existing Permission Group machinery is built for stable admin bundles while Crew has to tolerate daily churn, so reuse may cost more than it saves.

Does universal assignability make this a system-wide ticket after the MVP? The build is the same either way; the question is who owns it afterwards, and whether the forms and folders owners should be in the room at design rather than after it.

Who manages a crew with no supervisor? The crew supervisor stays optional, and the proposed fallback is the Site or Job supervisor field — which is information-only, so it carries no authority of its own.
If Location import goes ahead, offer to create crews from the people already in each Location.
scope: A crew has a name, members and an optional designated supervisor
Assigned to Sites and Jobs — a Site can hold several crews, and a crew can hold several Jobs at once
People can be added to a Site or a Job without a crew; a crew is how work is grouped, never a condition of being on site or signing in
Membership can be filled by rule at setup and is then saved; a live query would re-run against today's data and silently rewrite last month's record
Dated membership history
Coarse permissions on crew members — none, read-only, full edit — and grants only ever add
Access starts crew-based — on a crew, you see that crew; a site-wide view across every crew comes later
Pre-fills attendance, both the new component and the existing form field
Created on the web; people and crews can be moved between work contexts on mobile
tickets.evidence: 7 of 15 clients have no crew object and bend Location into one — three say so outright, and one invented a pseudo-asset purely to hold a crew's toolbox talk. A static roster fails on day one: crews are transient and move from project to project. Named Crew, not Group — decided, because Group collides with the existing Permission Group / Company Group feature in BIS Admin.

tickets.title: External people
tickets.summary: One record type for everyone who is not a user — a visitor, another trade on a shared site, a subcontractor's worker, a temporary worker, an auditor who signs. The same object with different things switched on, not five features. A person stored as free text can never hold training, can never be recognised on the next job, and has to be migrated before anything richer can attach to it, so the record exists from the first time someone is added.
tickets.slice: The MVP slice is a minimal record — name and company — plus training added by hand in this portal. It looks like a guest row on screen; underneath it is the same record the full ticket grows. The line between the two is portability: the slice stores training in one portal, the full ticket carries it across them.

related.note: External signers — a general contractor or an auditor — are a later variant. The existing external signature link may cover them first.

tickets.mvpNote: MVP-blocking through its slice — the same pattern as the forms-attribution ticket. Field Management owns it, and contractor management integrates after about six months of use, so nothing here waits on that conversation.
tickets.boundary: Not in the slice: login, a self-managed profile, cross-portal training, form filling, signing, permissions, crews, or charging. Contractor prequalification and company-level management belong to contractor management. Competency gating of external people belongs to the training ticket.
openQuestions: The identity rules are the only part that has to be decided before the slice is built: what makes someone the same person across projects and across different companies' portals, which company owns the record, and what happens if they later get a full account. They must not assume anything contractor management would have to undo.
Dev: are existing Site Access visitors stored as a record today, or as text? If a record, the slice may just be that record, extended.
Confirm with contractor management which objects they intend to reuse before the shape is locked.
Saving partway through becomes a real need the moment form filling is switched on — today's external links cannot save at all.
scope: A minimal record — name and company — visibly marked as external wherever it appears, and addable for a single day where that is all that is needed
It can go on an attendance list and on a work context; the visitors carried over from Site Access land here
Training added by hand, by an admin on the web or from the app on mobile — a topic, an expiry date and optionally a photo of the ticket, stored in this portal only
Stored as a record, not free text: adding the same person again on another day can point to the same record
tickets.evidence: External or no-login access is one of the four needs the research found that no internal framing had — about 5 companies in the corpus. At one client, other trades must sign and will never be users. At another, the workaround breaks two ways: someone logged into a different company's portal is refused access to the external form link, and external users cannot save, so half-finished submissions pile up. There is no memory between projects, so a contractor is asked to re-verify what he just filled out. On one shared project, 25 of about 50 of that client's people had to register in the other company's portal as well, and the client pays for half of them.

tickets.title: Training status
tickets.summary: A compliance badge, read from the training matrix. Wherever people are listed on a Site, a Job or a crew, each person carries a small badge — "3 outdated" — that links to their own training page, where the detail already lives. Field Management shows what the matrix already says and copies none of it. Nothing is set up here: no training requirements are attached to a Site or a Job, and the badge never blocks anyone from signing in, picking a Job or doing the work. The copy says training not current, never not competent — training is only a third of competency, and it is the only third the platform holds.

related.note: The badge shows beside each name as the supervisor marks presence. It shows; it never blocks — that is how the old conflict between these two was resolved. Exactly where it sits on the checklist is an open placement.
An external person has no training record of their own, so theirs is added by hand in this portal and the badge reads it exactly as it reads a user's.

blockedByAlso: Read access to the training matrix's compliance data, and to the existing expiry-reminder windows it already runs on.
tickets.mvpNote: MVP-blocking, and far smaller than it was. Off hold since the Oct 1 check-in: the badge ships with the MVP, the requirements engine and the entry gate are both gone, and assigning training by crew or job is a later matrix question — that matrix work alone was put at over 150 hours.
tickets.boundary: Field Management shows training; it neither assigns it nor holds requirements. Required topics stay in the training matrix, and assigning by crew or job comes later. The detail page is not rebuilt here — this is a badge and a link out, not a copy. Fixing the matrix's own expiry rules belongs to whoever owns it and must not be silently absorbed here: the badge is only ever as good as those rules. Nothing here gates entry; the existing access check stays behind the Access feature, untouched.
openQuestions: Which training the badge counts — required training only, or everything expired? A badge that surfaces training nobody needs for this work makes the list long and the signal weak.
Exactly where the badge appears: the crew list, the attendance checklist, the Site or Job people tab, and per person on supervisor mobile.
Who owns the expiry-rules problem in the matrix? Non-expiring courses against refresh cycles, and third-party courses whose rules cannot be changed.

Data fitness — a short spike before trusting the badge. At one client expiry is wrong in both directions: one topic never flags and another falsely flags. Nothing blocks any more, so a false flag costs attention rather than access — but it still costs trust.
Who adds an external person's training on mobile? External people have no login in the MVP, so it presumably means a supervisor photographing their ticket.
Dev: can this reuse the existing upload-certificate mechanism users already have on mobile, pointed at the external-person record instead of a user?
scope: A small badge per person — "3 outdated" — wherever people are listed on a Site, a Job or a crew
A count beside the missing-forms count, as its own number that never merges into it
The badge links to that person's own training page, which already holds the detail; Field Management copies none of it
Informational only — it never blocks a sign-in, a Job pick, or anything else
Read from the training matrix as it stands: no requirements are set on a Site or a Job, and no new training data model
"Expiring soon" follows the reminder windows the matrix already runs on; no new setting here
An external person's hand-entered training reads exactly like a user's record, so "no record" becomes actionable
tickets.evidence: 7 of 14 companies need to know who is cleared, and none of them is served at the point of work — they all find out late, and by hand. The two that gate hard do it in another system, so BIS is the evidence, not the gate. One client wants visibility rather than a gate, with warnings at 90, 60 and 30 days; another is against gating outright. Four clients did not raise it, and one did not discuss it at all — a hole in the data, not evidence against. What the badge answers is the seeing, which is the part nobody has. What it deliberately does not answer is the assigning, which is where the cost sits.

tickets.title: Forms report to the right work context
tickets.summary: Count a form toward the Site or Job the work was for — never the submitter's home location. A submission carries the work context it counts toward, independently of where the submitter is based or where they physically were. The data is often already on the submission; the gap is that the reporting layer cannot query it. Not a new hierarchy: an attribute clients already fill in that the system currently drops.
tickets.slice: Only the read path: Field Management can group and count forms by the work context the work was for, so the comparison knows which forms count toward which Site or Job.

related.note: Uses it, does not wait on it — one of the attribution paths reads the Job a worker selected.
Uses it, does not wait on it — another attribution path reads the ritual's attachment.

tickets.mvpNote: MVP-blocking — this slice has to ship for the comparison to be true. The full initiative, which is reporting group-by, cross-form roll-ups and retrofitting existing submissions, is post-MVP and not blocking.
tickets.boundary: Likely the first slice of something larger. Getting a form to report against the work context it was for is the same underlying problem as tying reports generally to the right place, and that larger initiative is not scoped and is not this ticket. What Field Management needs is only the read path; the reporting-layer half, where the client-visible payoff lands, ships on its own timeline.
openQuestions: The roughly ten-minute database check — the single biggest sizing question. Does the form-submission header carry its own location or node column, or is location always resolved through the user record? If it already has one, this ticket shrinks substantially. Open since August, and nothing should be estimated before it is answered.

Is every client's work-context field the same field? One carries a business unit, another links to a job, a third needs a customer site that does not exist as an object. With Sites and Jobs defined the likely answer is that they all become a work context — confirm per client.
What happens to existing submissions — backfill, leave as-is, or something between? It decides whether clients see corrected history or only a corrected future.

Can the slice ship on derived context alone, or does it need explicit selection too? A form filled outside any ritual would carry no work context and count toward nothing, which makes N outstanding wrong in the direction that erodes trust fastest: the work was done and the system still says it is missing.
Is the available-fields filter panel limited to one form at a time? About five minutes in the UI.
scope: The read path only — group and count submissions by the work context the work was for
A form started outside Field Management while someone is on a Job counts in both places: toward the Job, and in today's location reports, unchanged
tickets.evidence: Six clients across two corpora describe the same failure. This is the form-to-job link the six-anchors analysis names as the blocker for the job anchor — 4 of 15, the largest single anchor group — and now that Job sits inside the work-context engine, this is the ticket that makes those clients' numbers true. At one client the only link between a form and a job is a job number typed into the form's content, which is the structural defect that produces the retrieval pain. The biggest coverage lever in the backlog.

tickets.title: Scan an object to open the right form
tickets.summary: Scan the thing you are about to work on — a code on equipment, a vehicle, an extinguisher — and its form, task or folder opens with the context filled in. A context mechanism, not a presence mechanism: scanning yourself onto a site is the sign-in, and attendance owns that. It extends something that already works; the unblock is removing the requirement that the scanned thing be an owned asset.

related.note: Per-asset counting — the same asset link approached from the other direction.
Scanning into a place is a way into the sign-in that slice now owns, and the attendance form field has an existing QR option. Check what that option actually does before building a second mechanism.

blockedByAlso: The offline decision in the mobile ticket.
A pre-build code check — nothing here is honestly estimable until someone says where the owned-asset requirement is actually enforced.
tickets.blocksNote: Nothing waits on it. Site identification on mobile names scan as one mechanism among several, so without this it degrades to the others rather than failing — which is why that piece is a nice-to-have and this is Tier C.
tickets.mvpNote: Tier C — after the MVP, scheduled and not urgent. It makes the worker-facing entry point better; nothing critical waits on it.
tickets.boundary: Scanning yourself into a Site is attendance's job, not this ticket's — sign-in moved into Field Management when the access feature folded in. Geolocation and geofencing belong to the mobile ticket. Printing and sticking labels is client operations, and a customer object belongs to contractor management.
openQuestions: Where is the owned-asset requirement enforced, and what does a scan resolve against? The pre-build check — nobody has looked, and it is the cheapest unblocking action on the ticket.
Does BIS create the code, or read someone else's?
Must the scanned object exist in the system first?
Does scanning need the BIS app? One client will not install it — is a camera link into the browser possible?
Assets imported as Sites or Jobs — should their old codes point at the new work context, or keep pointing at the asset?
Is a Job code worth it? Picking from the list already works, so scanning only helps when the list is long.
What does the attendance field's existing QR option actually do? About five minutes in the UI.
tickets.evidence: Works today and is well liked. One client walks past a fire extinguisher, scans it, fills the form and moves on; another uses a vehicle code to make sure it is the right vehicle's form; at a third the helmet code was the most enthusiastically endorsed thing in the interview. The defensible framing comes from the code: an asset is the only thing in the platform that can own a location, own a form obligation and appear on a submission, which is why scanning is limited to assets — work contexts are the first new things that can hold what a scan resolves to.

tickets.title: Attendance — the presence record
tickets.summary: One presence record, and the supervisor checklist that fills it. It opens pre-filled from the crews assigned to a Site or a Job, and one supervisor marks people present or absent — no per-person device or login, which is the whole argument. Nobody needs a crew to be on the list. Sign-in and sign-out come in with it: they move out of the existing access feature and become this component, on any Site or Job, with their history migrated so past sign-ins still report. Every entry stores who, where, when, status, proof level and who recorded it. Signatures are in: where a client requires them, each person signs for themselves, on a passed-around device or on their own.
tickets.slice: Slice A of three, and the slice that keeps growing. The presence record, the supervisor checklist on Sites and Jobs, the "signed" proof level — which moved in from the last slice, because clients compare this with the form attendance field everyone already uses for signatures — and now sign-in and sign-out themselves, which came in with the access feature rather than waiting for Slice C.

related.note: The compliance badge shows beside each name as presence is marked. It shows; it never blocks — that is how the old conflict between these two was resolved. Exactly where it sits on the checklist is an open placement.

Scanning into a place is a way into the sign-in this slice now owns, and the existing attendance form field has a QR option of its own. Check what that option actually does before a second mechanism gets built.

tickets.mvpNote: MVP-blocking. The one supervisor action the research evidences — mark present, he's driving — is this checklist. Materially bigger than when it was first sized: signing moved in, and then sign-in and sign-out moved in on top of it.
tickets.boundary: Attendance capture only. The meeting object is its own ticket and reviewer sign-off is another. The access feature's own compliance check is not this ticket either — it stays behind the Access option, untouched. The new component and the existing attendance form field share no data path — deliberately and permanently, because bridging them means maintaining a route into something clients will leave on their own once the new one works better.
openQuestions: What do users actually see instead of "attendance"? Who's on site on a Site, who's on the job on a Job, attendees on a Meeting — the component is never named to users.

Why is the existing per-person signing not reaching clients — discoverability, defaults, scale, or a mobile gap? If a shipped capability is not being adopted, shipping more configurable capability does not fix it, and this initiative is about to ship a lot of it.

Does a regulator accept a sign-in as a signature, and are saved signatures legally acceptable? Both are compliance questions, and a supervisor must never be able to apply someone else's saved signature.
Dev, about ten minutes: is the attendee user-id on the existing per-attendee table nullable? It decides whether the old form field can hold external people; the new component holds them either way.

Dev, about ten minutes: is the per-signature timestamp stored, or only rendered? It decides whether one client's regulator finding is a default setting or a schema change — and a regulator flagged it, so it is the most urgent cheap unknown here.
Dev: can the new presence record extend the existing sign-in presence record, or does it sit alongside it and read from it?
scope: One presence record with the proof level stored from day one — marked by supervisor, signed in, signed — even though the minimum is set per use
The supervisor checklist, pre-filled from the crews on a Site or a Job, with add and remove; it is a starting point, not a lock
People can be added directly, with or without a crew — nobody needs a crew to sign in
Sign-in and sign-out, the who's-on-site list, timers and notifications move out of the existing access feature into this component, on any Site or Job
Existing sign-in history is migrated, so past sign-ins still report
People not yet recorded show as a gap, grouped by crew, so the gap is attributable — never as a blank
"Mark all present" is recorded as the supervisor's observation, never as an attestation on anyone's behalf
Selecting a Job or Site writes a presence entry, which is what makes that person owe that day's rituals there
Signatures — pass the device, or each person signs on their own; every signature stores who signed, when and on which device, reusing the existing mobile signature component rather than a new one
tickets.evidence: One person needs the app, not the whole crew, and the corpus makes that decisive: personal devices are banned in roughly 75% of areas at one client, field workers never reopen the app at another, 15 of 49 projects refuse it at a third, and a fourth will not install it at all. Per-attendee signing already exists in code — a dedicated attendee table, signature writes, outstanding-signature tracking, remote and deferred signing — so the capability is not missing. What is missing is recording presence without a form, filling the list without typing, and one record every way in writes to. One client rejects bulk-attest outright on legal grounds; another's loudest single ask is to stop making foremen retype 20–30 names, and that same client had no timestamps on its hazard-assessment entries, which the safety regulator flagged after an accident. 11 of 15 run safety meetings and 7 report specific pain.

tickets.title: Attendance — crew on the form field
tickets.summary: The existing attendance form field gains the ability to pre-fill its list from a Crew. Small, early, and independent of everything else in attendance — it is what stops foremen retyping 20–30 names. Today's nearest equivalent limits attendees to users at the same location as the assigning user, which is exactly the Location-overloading problem this initiative exists to fix.
tickets.slice: Slice B of three. Ships any time after Crew, independently of the presence record, and is much smaller than either of the other two.

related.note: The other half of the same ticket, and deliberately unconnected in the product — the form field and the new component share no data path.

tickets.mvpNote: Tier B — parallel build, active now, and it does not block the MVP. Small, and it removes the single most-complained-about piece of typing in the corpus.
tickets.boundary: This slice makes the old field less painful; it does not bridge the old field to the new component. Per-attendee signing on this field already works — only the filling is manual.
openQuestions: Dev, about ten minutes: is the attendee user-id on the existing per-attendee table nullable? If not, this field cannot hold external people, and that is a real limit on the quick win.
scope: The existing attendance form field can pre-fill its list from a Crew
Regression: existing attendance fields, per-attendee signing and remote signing behave exactly as today
tickets.evidence: One client's loudest single ask is to stop making foremen retype 20–30 names. The capability the field already has is per-person signing; what it lacks is any way to fill the list that is not typing, and the one filter that exists is scoped by location.

tickets.title: Scoped permissions — Can view
tickets.summary: A single read-only level, granted over a named set of Sites and Jobs — see what is owed, done and missing, and change nothing. It closes two clients' number one blocker at launch and needs no setup to reach. Built on the grant foundation the full model later extends: every grant has a subject, a crew or an individual, and a scope, a named set of work contexts — never the user's home location — and grants only ever add.
tickets.slice: The MVP slice. A safety manager one step removed from daily ownership, who needs to see several work contexts without editing them, is served at launch; the richer model follows after.
tickets.mvpNote: MVP-blocking. In the MVP only a client admin has full access and only a client admin grants "Can view", and a grant sends a notification, like sharing a file. Access starts crew-based alongside it: on a crew, you see that crew.
tickets.boundary: Sites and Jobs are the only scope type. Field Management's permissions are a clean sheet — they do not read from or change today's system roles, so the build must not lean on them. The coarse none / read-only / full edit on crew members belongs to the crew ticket, not here.
openQuestions: Is the additive union always safe? Grants only ever add, which avoids a precedence engine, but nobody has checked for a case where the union over-grants in a way a client would object to.
Is the scope only work contexts? Crews, forms and reports are plausible scopes, and adding a second scope type later is a schema change.
Curated views instead of raw access — rather than "has access to this", let admins curate what a safety manager sees. Raised and not settled.
No technical investigation stands behind this ticket. The technical-findings work covers attribution, attendance and rituals; it does not cover permissions. Treat the sizing as unevidenced.
scope: A grant has an explicit subject — an individual or a crew — and an explicit scope, a named set of Sites and Jobs
A read-only user can open everything in scope and change nothing; someone with no grant cannot see its records
A grant never reduces access a person already holds
Only a client admin grants it in the MVP, and the person or crew is notified
Regression: system roles behave exactly as today for anyone with no Field Management grant
A site-wide view — everything on a Site, across every crew — is deliberately not in this slice; access starts crew-based and that view comes with the full model
tickets.evidence: 6 clients, ranked number one by two of them. One client's record-validator is forced into full admin because there is nothing between learner and admin, and is now doing things she should not be doing. At another, the people who can view training can also edit it, which they call a big risk, and not seeing across locations is in their words by far their biggest problem right now. At a third the only available workaround breaks their payroll-system integration, so "they can already do this" is not true in practice.

tickets.title: Ritual
tickets.summary: What is owed. The model reads as what, applies to, trigger: the ritual is the bundle — forms, tasks and files linked from Folders — defined once centrally; it applies to a work context; and the trigger says when. In the MVP the only trigger is the schedule, built so sign-in, a set time or an incident can be added later. Cadence lives on the attachment, so one ritual runs daily at one site and weekly at another. A ritual is set once and left to run; one-off work is a task added or a form assigned inside the Site or Job, never a ritual.

related.note: A bundle can hold a meeting once both exist — scheduled toolbox talks. A toolbox talk is not a ritual example any more; it is a meeting.

tickets.mvpNote: MVP-blocking. It is what the gap view compares against.
tickets.boundary: Sites and Jobs only. Only recurring rituals can be outstanding; triggered ones like Incident have no cadence and never appear in the gap view. Assets themselves are never bundle content — link the asset's form instead, and that has moved out of the first phase anyway. One-off work is not a ritual: a random form on a Wednesday would make the ritual's reporting meaningless. Where one-off work is built — here, or as a link out to Folders — is now a company decision rather than this ticket's to make. Ritual sequencing and time windows are later.
openQuestions: The name. Product leadership dislikes "ritual" but offered no alternative — task and job are taken, and requirement implies something pre-existing. Worth revisiting alongside the module rename.
Uploading a standalone file with no Folders link is still open, and so is how clients without the Folders module reuse a file without storing copies.
Per arrival. One client does 1–10 per shift, per access point, and the MVP owes once per day per Job. Is per-arrival needed at launch, or is on-demand with no obligation honest for now?

Counting per asset is in scope but open — is listing assets on the attachment the right mechanism, or does it need a general asset-to-work-context link? The agreed priority order is forms, then files, then assets, and linking a form that belongs to an asset has now moved out of the MVP's first phase.
Do loose items modelled as a ritual of one cause any visible oddity in reporting?
A "duplicate this ritual" action, so one Site can have its own variation without changing everyone's — keep it, or leave it to the ritual page?
A meeting on both a Site and a Job at that Site — one meeting or two? Double counting has to be avoided either way.

Dev, about 25 minutes before estimating: what columns the existing form-frequency settings table carries, whether any working-days or operating-calendar table exists anywhere, and whether in-progress drafts can be read for a given obligation.

Required and optional items in a bundle — a proposal, not a decision. An optional item would work as on-demand: there if you need it, never counted as missing. It ties directly to where one-off work ends up living.
scope: The model — what, applies to, trigger. In the MVP the only trigger is the schedule, built so sign-in, a set time or an incident can be added later
Cadence vocabulary: fixed interval, working-days-only, use-triggered, metered, sub-day or shift-based
Freeform scheduling with exceptions
A starter ritual library so day one is not blank
Counts per person, per crew or per work context — set on the attachment, not on the bundle
Per-person obligations are owed by whoever signed in that day, on Sites as well as Jobs; a ritual counted per work context follows that work context's own calendar
Files linked from Folders, alongside forms and tasks. Forms that belong to an asset have moved out of the MVP's first phase
tickets.evidence: Cadence is not a recurrence rule. A daily check at a site that works 27 days in a 31-day month would count 31 days owed against 27 worked — 4 phantom misses per site, every month. The client was plain that the engine gets discarded if it does that.

tickets.title: Attendance — more places to attach
tickets.summary: More places the attendance component attaches: meetings, form witnesses, tasks. All of it writes to the same presence record the first slice builds, which is exactly why that record stores a proof level from day one rather than having one backfilled later.
tickets.slice: Slice C of three, and the one that keeps shrinking. The "signed" proof level used to live here and moved into Slice A, taking meetings and reviewer sign-off with it; sign-in and QR followed when the access feature folded into Field Management, so what is left is the attachment points.

related.note: A later place the component attaches. Meetings' own attendance no longer waits on this slice — it comes through the signed level in Slice A.

tickets.blocksNote: Nothing waits on it any more. Meetings and reviewer sign-off both used to, and both now point at Slice A instead.
tickets.mvpNote: Tier C — after the MVP, scheduled and not urgent.
tickets.boundary: Geolocation as a way in stays out: it asserts presence with no human action, needs an always-on permission that app-hostile crews will not grant, and fails for accuracy exactly where it is needed. The salvageable version is geo as corroboration — stamp the location when someone taps "I'm here".
openQuestions: Which attachment point is worth building first. Meetings is the only one with a ticket of its own, and it reads the presence record rather than this slice.
Are free-text guest attendees allowed anywhere outside the external-person record? If they are, "everyone signs beside their own name" has an unresolvable subset.
scope: The component attaching to meetings, to forms as witnesses, and to tasks
tickets.evidence: The attendance component only pays for itself once the same record is behind every place people are counted — a meeting, a witnessed form, a task. The ways in all landed earlier than planned: sign-in, sign-out and QR capture came into Slice A with the access feature, so what is left here is reach rather than capture.

tickets.title: Meetings
tickets.summary: The object behind a toolbox talk or a safety meeting: the topic, the documents, who was there, and each person's signature that they received it. It attaches to a Site or a Job, scheduled through a ritual or called on the spot, and it produces an exportable record that can leave BIS. A meeting is deliberately not a form — building it as a form template brings back the exact problem it exists to solve.

related.note: A ritual can include a meeting once both exist — that is how a meeting gets scheduled rather than called on the spot.
The calendar view lands on the mobile surface, and so does the offline session.
Shares the same sign-off component — built once, by whichever of the two lands first.

tickets.mvpNote: Tier C — after the MVP, and first in line after it. Built separately and added to Field Management. The signing it needs moved into the MVP, so its biggest dependency now lands earlier and it no longer drags a later slice forward into the release.
tickets.boundary: Not a form, and not a general meeting system — no invites, RSVPs, minutes or agenda workflow. The sign-off component itself is not built here: it is built once, by whichever of attendance or reviewer sign-off ships first. The calendar belongs to mobile and to the parent's own scope item.
openQuestions: Is "led by" needed? No client asked for it directly — an optional field, or cut?
One meeting, several Jobs. One client runs one toolbox talk for six jobs. Does the meeting count toward each Job, or only the Site? Double counting has to be avoided either way.
The label — a short list written by BIS, as Sites and Jobs have, or a client-typed label? And which words go on the list?

Is this still worth building once self-signing lands? The challenge on record is that the only difference from a Site's attendance may be the notes. The research says the content half is exactly what is missing, so the lean is to build it — but re-check once signing exists.
Nobody has sized it. An estimate is needed before it can be scheduled, and the one reaction on record is a reaction, not an estimate.
A meeting on both a Site and a Job at that Site — one meeting or two?
scope: A name, the topic or agenda notes, supporting documents or photos, and who led it
People pre-filled from the crews on that Site or Job, including external people
Each person signs that they received it — the default minimum is "signed", and a client can lower it to marked-by-supervisor with a warning
An exportable record that can leave BIS, for a general contractor, an auditor or a regulator
Reporting on who attended which one
tickets.evidence: Product leadership wants it and rates it highly — daily safety meetings happen everywhere and there is no good way to handle it. The signing half is easy; the content half is the gap. Scoping a meeting to a crew is also what fixes one client's chase-everyone problem: today toolbox talks go out company-wide and someone then checks who has not signed, one person at a time. 11 of 15 run toolbox talks, the most common ritual in the corpus.

tickets.title: Scoped permissions — the full model
tickets.summary: Richer permission shapes than none / read-only / full edit, over a named set of work contexts. Two interaction models are on the table and the room picks one: a share sheet, where you choose a subject and an access level; or named custom roles with a view/edit checklist per object type, granted over a set of Sites and Jobs. Custom roles is the lean — it is what the trio agreed and what clients describe — and the share sheet is the cheaper option with nothing to set up.
tickets.slice: The second slice. It extends the "Can view" grant foundation rather than replacing it, which is why the MVP slice had to be built on that foundation in the first place.

related.note: Grants to contractors and visitors — what an external person is allowed to do — come through this model, after the MVP.

tickets.mvpNote: Tier B — parallel build, active now, and it does not block the MVP. What is open is not whether it ships but which interaction model it ships as. Product leadership's read: system-wide custom roles are a large build, but building it out of the box inside a new module is acceptable.
tickets.boundary: The system-wide custom-permissions overhaul this splits off from is a separate initiative and is not in scope, and neither is retrofitting segmentation into existing pages. External and contractor users come with contractor management. Where the real need is a dashboard rather than a grant, this is the wrong ticket.
openQuestions: Option A or Option B — share sheet or custom roles? The room decides, not this document. Option A is cheaper and needs zero setup to reach "can view"; Option B is more capable at the cost of an admin building roles before anyone benefits. No meeting on record has picked one.
How rich is "richer"? A view/edit split per object type, per screen, or per field? Undecided, and it is the main sizing lever — effectively the same question as Option A or B.

Validate the ask before counting a client. Sometimes what a client calls a permissions problem is really a reporting problem; one example turned out to need a dashboard, not a grant. That costs one question per client and could shrink the ticket materially.
Who hands out grants after the MVP — can a supervisor share read-only access themselves?
A Site or Job supervisor — a grant, or a field on the work context?

The three-level ceiling on the share-sheet option: a client who needs a fourth level has nowhere to go until the system-wide version exists. Say that out loud, or the first client to hit it reads it as a bug.
What shape the site-wide manager view takes — everything on a Site, across every crew. It was deferred to this model when access was set to start crew-based, and nobody has drawn it.
scope: Option A — a share sheet: full access, can edit, can view, granted to a subject over a scope
Option B — named custom roles with a view/edit checklist per object type, granted over a named set of work contexts
Whichever wins: view and edit are separable, and grants still only ever add
Regression: system roles behave exactly as today for anyone with no grant, and the MVP's read-only slice keeps working either way
tickets.evidence: The pattern clients want already exists elsewhere — one client demoed another platform mid-interview, picking exactly what people could and could not see rather than accepting pre-canned roles. Contractor management needs the same thing on contractor sites, for roughly half of the clients interviewed for it. Building segmentation into a module that has no pages yet costs a fraction of retrofitting it into pages that do — an argument, not a measurement: nobody has estimated either half.

tickets.title: Mobile
tickets.summary: Field Management in the app. Supervisors see the state of the work contexts their crew is assigned to and fix it from the same screen; workers get a "today" filter over the lists they already use, plus the list of Sites and Jobs to pick from. One ticket, one platform, one team. Grouped by ritual, exactly as the web is — two groupings of one dataset is how people stop trusting the number. Worker-side is pull, never push.

related.note: Scan is one of the nice-to-have ways of working out where someone is. For Jobs the list is already the mechanism, so this degrades rather than fails.

blockedByAlso: The parent's comparison logic — mobile shows calculated state, it does not calculate it.
The offline decision — sync, or degrade. This is the blocking decision, and it is not made.
tickets.maturity: No end user or supervisor was interviewed. All 15 interviews were with admins, so every claim here about what a supervisor or worker wants is a safe bet, not evidence. Say so every time this ticket is presented.
tickets.mvpNote: MVP-blocking — the supervisor surface in full, and the worker surface as a small slice. It no longer waits on scoped permissions: a supervisor sees the work contexts their crew is assigned to, built entirely from Crew. The gap view is in the MVP on the app as well as the web, so this ticket carries it too.
tickets.boundary: Not work dispatch. No time-of-day push, never delivered as assignments, and it has to tolerate late and backdated submissions. Fixing things is on both platforms; creating things is web-only, so Sites and Jobs are not created on mobile in the MVP.
openQuestions: Offline: sync or degrade? Either the obligation set syncs to the device or the mobile surface degrades to something that works offline. One client runs 50–80% no-signal sites; at another, operators go days without connectivity. This is the blocking decision and it needs its own working session.
One person on up to ten work contexts in a day. How does every screen work for someone holding one and for someone holding ten?
Who adds an external person's training on mobile, given external people have no login? Presumably a supervisor photographing the ticket.
Per-person detail — tapping a person to see their arrival, how presence was recorded, and what they owe here. In the MVP or not, and scoped to this work context only if so?
A supervisor calendar view — wanted in both trio meetings. In the MVP, or after?

Signer identity on a shared phone. Signing cannot rely on who is logged in, so it needs a lightweight identify-the-signer step rather than a full logout and login. Check the existing remote-signing path first; the question may go away rather than need solving.
Which team and repo own this? The app is a different codebase from the backend, so this may need splitting by repo even though it is one product surface.
scope: A. Supervisor — state first and names second, grouped by ritual, with three states on every obligation and the compliance badge beside missing forms, read from the training matrix and linking out to each person's own training page
A. Supervisor actions, edit but not create — mark present, collect signatures, add or remove people for today, move a ritual for this work context only, move people and crews
B. Worker — a "today" filter over the lists they already use, and the list of Sites and Jobs to pick from; picking one is the sign-in, and it starts their day on it
B. Direction, not locked: a "your day" home screen woven into the app rather than a separate page
C. Working out where someone is — scan and geolocation stay nice-to-have; geolocation suggests, it never transforms
D. Web against mobile decided deliberately rather than inherited — fixing on both, creating on the web
E. Who's on the field — sign-in and sign-out, the live list, timers and notifications, moved over from the existing access feature. ⏳ In the MVP, or just after?
tickets.evidence: One client's number one ask is explicitly mobile. A field-facing admin at another has to leave the app for mobile web to read a colleague's submission. At a third, bulk-adding attendees is web-only — the highest-volume, most time-critical task sits on the platform the foreman is not holding. The reliable mobile user is the supervisor, not the worker, and the worker surface is deliberately small because the demand is real while the reach is not: devices banned in roughly 75% of areas at one client, workers who never reopen the app at another, 15 of 49 projects refusing it at a third, and an outright install refusal at a fourth.

tickets.title: Reviewer sign-off
tickets.summary: A qualified person confirms a completed form is OK — without editing it, reopening it, or being assigned to it in advance. The form stays exactly as submitted; the sign-off records who, when, which version they saw, and an optional note. The request keeps arriving as "let us edit completed forms", and this is the answer to it: reviewers get what they need without opening up editing, which would let one person change another's answers.

related.note: A crew can be the "who" — a group whose job is to sign off, moving between places without a fixed schedule.
External signers such as a general contractor or an auditor. The existing external signature link may cover them first.
Shares the same sign-off component.

tickets.maturity: The evidence is thinner than for the rest of the initiative. The two strongest asks came through client services and through one interview outside the 15-interview study, and the details of the strongest one are relayed second-hand rather than in the client's own words. Enough to justify a ticket; not enough to size it big.
tickets.mvpNote: Tier B — start now, independently of the MVP, because a client is waiting. It is not part of the Field Management release: it does not wait for it, and Field Management does not wait for it. It works on any completed form. The sign-off component it shares with attendance is already being designed through another ticket, reusing the existing mobile signature component, so the order-of-work worry that hung over this has largely answered itself.
tickets.boundary: Not editing completed forms, and not a replacement for form stages — stages keep working for clients who want the form to wait. Required sign-off sequences would turn this back into a workflow. Documents that are not forms, and approving training records, are separate questions.
openQuestions: Who may sign off, before the full permission model exists? A setting on the form template — "these roles can sign off" — or a crew. The template setting is closest to what exists today.
Can a ritual require sign-off? If it can, a Field Management item is not done until it is signed off, which is useful but adds a new state to the gap view.
Can a form template require a number of sign-offs?
Send back, or just note? A formal "needs changes" status would notify the submitter — and starts to look like a stage, which is the thing this avoids.
Documents as well as forms? Reading and acknowledging a policy is closer to the meeting object than to form review.
Which sub-department owns it — this module, or Forms? It works on every form.
Dev, before sizing: is the existing "request signature on stage complete" option most of the way there? If a stage can be made non-blocking, the ticket may shrink considerably.
scope: A sign-off on a completed form recording who signed, a persisted timestamp, which version they saw, and an optional note
People are permitted to sign off by form template and place, as individuals or as a crew — never assigned per form
Several sign-offs per form, each with its own timestamp; in the first version order does not matter and none waits on another
A form edited after a sign-off shows that sign-off as applying to an earlier version
Forms waiting for my sign-off appear in the existing to-do, not in a new list and not inside Field Management
Reporting: signed off or not, by whom and when, plus a list of completed forms still waiting
tickets.actionFlag: Start now — a client is waiting
tickets.evidence: Two direct asks — one relayed through a sprint meeting, one from an interview outside the 15-client study — plus one more through client services, one direct corpus case, one client who does it outside BIS entirely, and three adjacent cases. The sharpest shape: a supervisor makes unannounced visits and needs to sign off the daily hazard assessment after arriving, because the crew completed it before they got there and the only company tablet on site belongs to the foreperson. What is missing is a signature that sits beside a finished form, from someone who was not pre-assigned. The newest ask is a client wanting to sign off compliance on procedures held in Folders, and that is the ticket the shared component is being designed through.

tickets.title: Field Management MVP
tickets.summary: The parent ticket. It carries the full MVP scope and links every child, so QA, reviewers and stakeholders can see the whole project in one place. Done, in client terms: a safety manager opens Field Management and sees her Sites and Jobs, each reading current or N outstanding with the training count beside it. She clicks one and sees what it owed this period against what was done — grouped by ritual, broken down by job and by crew. And she built almost nothing to get there.
tickets.blocksNote: It is the end of the graph — everything else flows into it.
tickets.mvpNote: This is the MVP. It ships when its nine Tier A blockers ship. The training badge came off hold at the Oct 1 check-in and was cut down to a badge read from the training matrix, so the nine is now nine rather than eight and a question.
tickets.boundary: A record and omission layer, not a work-dispatch tool. Don't build a place to work; build a place that proves work happened and says what's missing. It is a paid module with a free trial period, which is what makes the overlap with Folders and Assets a company decision rather than a scoping one. The honest limit: a client whose places are all Locations gets less on day one until live-linked Locations land, and those cannot slip far behind the MVP.
openQuestions: Offline — sync or degrade? The blocking decision for mobile, and a roughly 30-minute working session closer to build.
Uploading a standalone file to a ritual, without Folders — in or out? Files linked from Folders are in.
Rituals counting per asset — in scope, still open. Linking a form that belongs to an asset has moved out of the MVP's first phase.
Saved signatures — check with compliance before build.
Setup — Sites and Jobs in one pass, or one kind at a time?
Who adds a visitor's training on mobile?
Check the status of the two existing Site Access scan-in/out tickets — reusing the Site Access site object brings a timing risk back.
The name "Ritual" — still a working name.
scope: 1. Work contexts index — one row per Site or Job, state as the leftmost visual, with the compliance count beside it as a separate number
2. Single work-context view — this period's obligations grouped by ritual, broken down by job and by crew
3. Day one — pick the kinds and their labels, existing sites already there, import from Assets, attach a starter ritual

4. Surfacing what's outstanding — the gap view, on the web and in the app, in the MVP. A ranking rule, not a screen; a draft counts as outstanding, labelled in progress. It may become a platform-wide pattern
5. Why it counted — who submitted it, their home location, the work context it counts toward, and how that was decided
6. Job close-out — awaiting close, confirm, close-out, then the exportable evidence pack
7. Notification triggers — on the existing email and text rails, conservative defaults, no time-of-day push
8. Calendar view and past-day lookup — low priority
9. One-off assignment — add a task or assign a form inside a Site or Job, counting toward it. ⏳ Whether that is built here or linked out to Folders is a company decision

10. Who's on the field — sign-in and sign-out, the live list, timers and notifications, Field Management's own now and moved over from the access feature with their history migrated. ⏳ In the MVP, or just after?
Commercial — a paid module with a free trial period. ⏳ The overlap with Folders and with Assets needs a company decision before those parts are built
Release materials, agreed but not a ticket: documentation and a knowledge base, a webinar, onboarding videos, and an in-product tour
tickets.evidence: The risk that outranks every ticket is setup burden. A safety lead with 52 branches was handed a working setup path for her own number one pain and never did it — it was simply too much. If the best-case user will not set it up, nobody will, so every decision is measured against what a client gets on day one with zero setup. Around 7 independent clients describe the same core need, which makes it the best-corroborated finding in the study. And every interview was with an admin: no supervisors, no field workers, so everything about what they want is a safe bet rather than evidence.
